content: Laudanum is a tincture of opium, often sweetened with sugar, and historically referred to as wine of opium. In the 16th century, the Swiss physician Paracelsus explored the medicinal properties of opium. He recognized its significant analgesic (pain-relieving) effects and named it laudanum, derived from the Latin word laudare (to praise) or possibly from labdanum (a plant extract). However, Paracelsus was unaware of its addictive potential. During this period, the limited pharmacopoeia made opium derivatives some of the most effective treatments available. Consequently, laudanum was widely prescribed for a variety of conditions, ranging from colds to meningitis to cardiac diseases, and it was used in both adults and children. It was also employed during the yellow fever epidemic. Laudanum became particularly popular during the Romantic and Victorian eras in Europe and the United States. Initially considered a working-class drug, it was cheaper than gin or wine because it was classified as a medication and not taxed as an alcoholic beverage. Many notable literary figures were known to use laudanum, including Lord Byron, Jane Johnston Schoolcraft, Kate Chopin, Samuel Taylor Coleridge (who struggled with addiction for much of his life), Thomas De Quincey (who wrote Confessions of an English Opium-Eater), Percy Bysshe Shelley (who experienced severe hallucinations from laudanum), John Keats, Lewis Carroll (whose work Alice in Wonderland may have been influenced by it), and Edgar Allan Poe. Other users included Mary Todd Lincoln, who was misprescribed laudanum for sleep issues, leading to anxiety, hallucinations, and eventual institutionalization. Political figures such as George Washington, William Wilberforce, and Meriwether Lewis also reportedly used the drug. In Victorian society, laudanum was commonly prescribed to women for menstrual cramps and vague aches. It was also used to achieve the pale complexion associated with tuberculosis, which was considered desirable at the time. Nurses even administered laudanum to infants. Tragically, Elizabeth Siddal, a Pre-Raphaelite muse, died from a laudanum overdose. Laudanum has been depicted in numerous works of fiction. In literature, it appears in William Faulkner's Pylon, Thomas Harris's Hannibal Rising, Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey–Maturin series, Alan Moore's The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, among others. It is also referenced in Gabriel García Márquez's Love in the Time of Cholera and One Hundred Years of Solitude, as well as in Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone. In Interview with the Vampire by Anne Rice, laudanum is used as a means of poisoning. The drug is also mentioned in works by Charles Dickens, James Joyce, and Sarah Waters, among others. In film, laudanum plays a role in From Hell, where it is used by both Jack the Ripper and Inspector Frederick Abberline. It is also featured in Cold Mountain, Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World, and Sense and Sensibility. In Tombstone, Mattie Blaylock, Wyatt Earp's common-law wife, is depicted as a laudanum addict, reflecting her real-life struggles. On television, laudanum is portrayed in series such as Deadwood, Hornblower, and Little House on the Prairie. In The Simpsons, Mr. Burns humorously includes laudanum on his shopping list. In music, laudanum has inspired various artists. It is the name of a French electronic project by Matthieu Malon and is referenced in songs by The Decemberists, Cradle of Filth, and Shane MacGowan, among others. Today, laudanum remains available by prescription in the United States, classified as a Schedule II controlled substance. Its most common formulation is deodorized tincture of opium (DTO), which contains 10 milligrams of morphine per milliliter. Deodorized opium has had the alkaloid narcotine removed, as it lacks analgesic properties and often causes nausea and stomach upset. Laudanum is primarily used to treat severe diarrhea and pain. However, caution is necessary to avoid confusion between opium tincture (laudanum) and camphorated opium tincture (paregoric), as the former is significantly more potent. Misuse or dosing errors can lead to overdose. The U.S. Pharmacopeia advises against abbreviating deodorized tincture of opium as DTO to prevent such errors.
